bounty.title: Donation/funding for german language
bounty.body:
Hi there, 

*tl;dr: click on opire link to add funding/donation for german language.*

### I) Motivation for german language in kokoro
#### I.1) Kokoro is best quality openweight TTS
See, e.g. the leaderboards:
- https://artificialanalysis.ai/text-to-speech/leaderboard?open-weights=true
- https://huggingface.co/spaces/TTS-AGI/TTS-Arena
- https://huggingface.co/spaces/TTS-AGI/TTS-Arena-V2

#### I.2) Kokoro is efficient (and fast, CPU only possible)
It can be run on CPU using streaming. Most of the even lesser openweight competitors use much more resources or may need a graphics card to even run the ai models (while still beeing less good).


*The current 10 top openweight tts on artificialanalysis are not suitable* (see comparison table, using ai searches).

 <details>
    <summary>Comparison table</summary>

| # | Model | Typical hardware requirements (inference) | CPU real‑time viability* | German support (out‑of‑the‑box)** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Kokoro 82M v1.0 | Very small (~tens of M params). Runs on CPU or small GPU (≈2–4 GB VRAM). | High – real‑time or near real‑time on a modern CPU. | Unclear / probably no official DE voice in base models. |
| 2 | Fish Speech 1.5 | Medium–large; GPU strongly recommended (≈10–12 GB VRAM for smooth use). | Low – CPU works but far from real‑time. | No clear German support; mainly EN/zh focus. |
| 3 | Maya1 | Large multi‑billion‑param model; needs high‑end GPU (≥16 GB VRAM). | Very low – practical real‑time on CPU not expected. | Unclear – no solid public info about German at cutoff. |
| 4 | Chatterbox | Several variants; Multilingual / Turbo ≈few‑hundred‑M params; GPU (≈8 GB) recommended, CPU possible. | Medium – Turbo/distilled variant can approach RT on a strong CPU; full multilingual is slower. | Yes – multilingual checkpoints explicitly include German. |
| 5 | Zonos‑v0.1 | Medium–large; designed for GPU inference (≈8 GB+ VRAM recommended). | Very low – CPU inference is slow, not interactive. | No – appears English‑only in public releases. |
| 6 | VibeVoice 7B | Very large (7B). Requires powerful GPU(s), typically ≥16–24 GB VRAM. | Effectively none – CPU real‑time is not realistic. | Likely multilingual, but exact DE status not confirmed. |
| 7 | OpenVoice v2 | Medium; CPU possible but GPU (≈6–8 GB+ VRAM) recommended for cloning speed / latency. | Low–medium – typical CPUs are slower than real‑time; strong CPU + heavy tuning might get close. | Unclear – paper stresses EN/zh/ja; DE status uncertain. |
| 8 | Step TTS Mini | Small / edge‑oriented; runs well on CPU or very small GPU (≈2–4 GB VRAM). | High – explicitly designed to run fast on CPU. | No official German – docs only confirm zh + EN. |
| 9 | XTTS v2 (Coqui) | Medium; GPU with ≥8 GB VRAM recommended for smooth multilingual / cloning use. | Low–medium – CPU possible but usually >RT latency. | Yes – XTTS v2 is explicitly multilingual incl. German. |
| 10 | StyleTTS 2 | Medium–large; practical use assumes GPU with ≈8–12 GB VRAM. | Very low – CPU inference is slow, not real‑time. | Base models EN‑only; DE only via community fine‑tunes. |

  </details>
(Most suitable for german by a fair amount is chatterbox multilingual which is 500M - but it isn't really suitable; Kokoro with german is higher value)

#### I.3) There is high demand/ many requests

a) See how active that threads have been:
https://github.com/hexgrad/kokoro/issues/232
https://github.com/hexgrad/kokoro/issues/186

b) Also german is one of the language in europa with many [speakers like 95 million L1 and 85 million L2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language).

c) Also you can see in the table, there are no TTS alternatives.

### II) Funding

#### II.1) Funding movitation
*This issue is about funding the german language.* There have been many comments, but all in all it probably didn't help much @hexgrad to add the german language, because he has some specific needs for the training data. The common voice isn't e.g. viable as I read somewhere by him. Having the effort of grabbing all the data together is not efficient for him.

***So, it's probably most straight forward to fund him the money to produce the german training data like he needs it (using other TTS) and train the model.***

#### II.2) Funding method
I considered polar.sh, algora and opire (had some options listed by ai). I found opire most straightforward to start, so I'm using that. *But feel free to also add other ones to this thread*. Also correct me, if something is not correctly configured.

#### II.3) Donation/Funding
Let's go. And see how much we can get together, to support hexgrad in adding german:

https://app.opire.dev/issues/01KCKZCP14P37WZQZQA9W6BGJJ

You can login via github. See that as an coordination plattform. You can use Stripe but you may also pay via paypal if you want, without directly using the plattform ( I spoke with the apparent developer), but I would say that with a question mark (disclaimer).

~You login with github and pay with PayPal, VISA, SEPA using Stripe. *Don't make an Stripe Express account via option link as that is for business people*. Use a normal account https://dashboard.stripe.com/register?locale=de-DE  .~

~***I'm currently trying to figure out it myself (using Opire for the first time), so you might want (and I recommend that) to subscribe this thread and wait before i figured it out. I write a message, after i got the payment mechanism to work (at first, I wrongly created a stripe express acount, so i need to try the normal stripe account myself after i deleted the express account, which needs contacting).***~

👉 Got a pull request resolving this? Claim the bounty by commenting `/claim #290` in your PR and joining `algora.io`
How much guys do you need to support German voice?

We have released a German model. The quality is far from perfect, and it only supports two voices: one male and one female.

https://huggingface.co/Tundragoon/Kokoro-German
Really appreciate the effort, Thomcle. It sounds a bit off, though.

Basically "we" need is a **misaki[de]** package which generates the phonemes for the written German language. The German kokoro version from tomcle does not do this *yet*, **but** provided the correct phonemes existing models may just work.
/try

/try

**Implementation Plan for #290**

**What needs to be done:**
Add German language support to Kokoro TTS by registering German (`'d'`) as a new language code, wiring it through the G2P pipeline via espeak-ng (which already supports German), training German voice embeddings, and publishing voice `.pt` files to the HuggingFace model repo.

**Files I will modify:**
- `kokoro/pipeline.py` — Add `'de': 'd'` and `'de-de': 'd'` to `ALIASES` dict (line 11); add `d='de'` to `LANG_CODES` under the espeak-ng section (line 28). German will use the existing `espeak.EspeakG2P` fallback path at line 141, no special G2P branch needed.
- `kokoro/__main__.py` — Add `"d"` (German) to the `languages` list (line 23).
- `kokoro.js/src/voices.js` — Register new German voice entries (e.g., `df_*`, `dm_*`) with metadata (language `"de"`, gender, quality grades).
- HuggingFace repo `hexgrad/Kokoro-82M` — Upload trained German voice `.pt` files under `voices/` directory (e.g., `df_clara.pt`, `dm_hans.pt`).

**Approach:**
1. **Code registration** is straightforward: German maps to espeak-ng language code `'de'`, which the existing `EspeakG2P` path already handles. No custom misaki module is needed — espeak-ng has robust German phonemization.
2. **Voice training** is the core effort: generate high-quality German speech training data (likely using a commercial TTS as seed data per hexgrad's established workflow), then fine-tune/train Kokoro voice embeddings to produce `[510, 256]` style tensors stored as `.pt` files. Target at least one male and one female German voice.
3. **Validation**: verify German phoneme coverage against the model's existing vocabulary (`kokoro/model.py` vocab mapping), ensure text chunking at the 510-phoneme limit works correctly for German text patterns, and test end-to-end synthesis quality.

**Estimated time:** 40-60 hours (primarily voice data preparation and model training; code changes themselves are ~2 hours)
/try
/attempt
/try

Hey folks,

Like many of you, I've been amazed by the Kokoro-82M TTS model. But when I tried to find a guide on how to actually fine-tune it for a new language, I hit a wall. There wasn't really a public training recipe available. So, I decided to see how hard it could be to figure it out myself.

After about a week of throwing GPU hours and LLM tokens at the problem, I somehow managed to vibe-reverse-engineer a working training pipeline using a patched version of StyleTTS2. 

The good news: The end-to-end pipeline actually works! Stage 1 training produces intelligible German speech through the standard Kokoro inference pipeline. I've documented all the PyTorch API migrations (like updating weight_norm), token mappings, and training bugs I had to fix to make StyleTTS2 output Kokoro-compatible weights.

The bad news: I am way out of my depth on Stage 2 (the prosody predictor). Stage 2 currently degrades the style_encoder and outputs static noise, likely because joint_epoch=999 leaves it unoptimized while its buffers drift. I built a workaround script that stitches the Stage 1 style encoder together with the Stage 2 predictor, but I don't have the ML expertise to properly fix the adversarial GAN/SLM training loop natively.

I took the time to clean everything up and open-sourced the full training guide, the patched StyleTTS2 submodule, and all my scripts here:

👉 https://github.com/semidark/kokoro-deutsch

If anyone with actual ML experience wants to take a look, laugh at my messy approach, or help figure out the Stage 2 settings, I'd hugely appreciate it. I hope this serves as a good jumping-off point for anyone else trying to train custom Kokoro voices!

/attempt 

Success! We’ve found the training recipe for Kokoro and are now activly working on German voice packs. The scripts and process are in the [semidark/kokoro-deutsch repo](https://github.com/semidark/kokoro-deutsch), allowing the community to create German voice packs or train Kokoro on other data.

Unfortunately, we can’t submit a PR and directly claim the price, since we went beyond the initial goal of funding a German dataset for Hexgard and, by accident, fully liberated Kokoro’s training process. 

Ups... 🫣 I'll take the money anyway 😈

**For context on the timeline here**

On April 10, I published [semidark/kokoro-deutsch](https://github.com/semidark/kokoro-deutsch) -- a complete training recipe for fine-tuning Kokoro for German, including a patched StyleTTS2 pipeline, dataset preparation scripts, and checkpoint conversion tools. I announced it [in this thread](https://github.com/hexgrad/kokoro/issues/290#issuecomment-4223937723) the same day.

Over the following days (April 10-14), I fixed critical Stage 2 training bugs (DataParallel ordering, weight loading, adversarial training), and a community formed around the repo. @dida-80b and @ichDaheim contributed significant GPU time to produce actual trained German models -- here's an [intermediate inference example](https://huggingface.co/datasets/junkstage/kokoro_training/blob/main/bernd_stage1_epoch58.wav). A multi-speaker base model has since been [published on HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/dida-80b/kokoro-deutsch-hui-base).

PR #316 was opened on April 17 -- one week after my repo went public. It adds pipeline wiring and a text normalizer, but no trained model or training recipe. The pipeline wiring (lang_code='d', ALIASES, LANG_CODES) is the same approach I implemented in my fork and which was already described in earlier comments on this thread.

I had planned to submit a PR myself after cleaning up the code from a weekend of intensive work. I'll be putting one together that includes the pipeline integration along with reference to the actual training infrastructure and trained voices that make German TTS functional, not just wired up.

> It looks like the current openweight TTS options for German are lacking quality and efficiency compared to Kokoro. I can train a high-quality German language model for Kokoro by curating and processing a suitable German audio dataset. I've previously built robust data pipelines for speech synthesis projects. If this is still open, I'd be happy to submit a PR for a bounty: https://github.com/ericjoye

@ericjoye
Same here, but I am more on it because I want the Product not the bounty. But still, come join the https://github.com/semidark/kokoro-deutsch project/community. We are already working hard on getting this done. Training recipe,  datasets (synthetic, human and hybrid) and Models are all in the working. 

Actually we are almost there, but more hands will help getting it done more quickly. 🚀

Not sure, maybe you have a look on what we are currently working on dataset wise and tell me if it tickles a fancy with you. 


**Dataset and Model training is coordinated here**

https://github.com/semidark/kokoro-deutsch/issues/4 
https://github.com/semidark/kokoro-deutsch/issues/9

Hi! I would love to take on this bounty for German language support. I am reviewing the current phonemizer implementation and the dataset requirements. I'll get started right away on the grapheme-to-phoneme mapping and integration.

> Hi! I would love to take on this bounty for German language support. I am reviewing the current phonemizer implementation and the dataset requirements. I'll get started right away on the grapheme-to-phoneme mapping and integration.

Lol. Actually that already has been solved by kokoro-deutsch. But feel free to reinvent from scratch. 😅

> > Hi! I would love to take on this bounty for German language support. I am reviewing the current phonemizer implementation and the dataset requirements. I'll get started right away on the grapheme-to-phoneme mapping and integration.
> 
> Lol. Actually that already has been solved by kokoro-deutsch. But feel free to reinvent from scratch. 😅

@semidark — Yes, exactly! I should have been clearer — I'm already working **in your `kokoro-deutsch` repo**, not here. This comment was just to register upstream.

In `semidark/kokoro-deutsch#4` I've already posted a detailed breakdown of the pipeline I'm building. To summarize what's in progress:
- **`misaki_de` G2P module** — drop-in replacement for `misaki` with IPA exception dictionary for modern loanwords
- **Full Docker pipeline** — HUI Corpus (Hokuspokus) + F5-TTS augmentation + WhisperX alignment  
- **`lang_code='d'`** patch for `hexgrad/kokoro/pipeline.py`

The dataset pipeline is running now. Looking forward to submitting a PR to your repo soon!

The detailed breakdown:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c2cfe9c2-0bcf-4deb-8783-04502b667675)

🫠

> The detailed breakdown:
> 
> ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c2cfe9c2-0bcf-4deb-8783-04502b667675)
> 
> 🫠

Haha, yeah guilty as charged 🕵️‍♂️ AI helps me organize my thoughts and structure the proposal, but the pipeline code is 100% real and already running locally! 🚀

Speaking of the pipeline, I'm hitting a wall with the data acquisition step. The official IISYS server hosting the HUI Hokuspokus dataset (10.7 GB) is extremely unstable. It keeps dropping the connection and doesn't support proper byte-range resumes, which results in a corrupted zip file every single time. I've tried downloading it 4 times using different tools.

Could anyone mirror Hokuspokus.zip to a more stable host (like HuggingFace, Google Drive, or AWS) or at least split it into multi-part chunks (e.g., 1GB each)? It's the only blocker I have right now to start processing the audio.

@avtosubaru25 
> Haha, yeah guilty as charged 🕵️‍♂️ AI helps me organize my thoughts and structure the proposal, but the pipeline code is 100% real and already running locally! 🚀

Congrats bruh with the pipeline. But I am afraid you are a little late to that party. At least a dozen people are running this in different setups on their local hardware since we open-sourced the training recipe 2 weeks ago. What exactly is the news here?

My advice, if I may: Invest your LLM tokens in a different bounty. This one probably is stale and won't be paid out anyhow.

But take this as you will.

It can be run on CPU using streaming. Most of the even lesser openweight competitors use much more resources or may need a graphics card to even run the ai models (while still beeing less good).


*The current 10 top openweight tts on artificialanalysis are not suitable* (see comparison table, using ai searches).

 <details>
    <summary>Comparison table</summary>

| # | Model | Typical hardware requirements (inference) | CPU real‑time viability* | German support (out‑of‑the‑box)** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Kokoro 82M v1.0 | Very small (~tens of M params). Runs on CPU or small GPU (≈2–4 GB VRAM). | High – real‑time or near real‑time on a modern CPU. | Unclear / probably no official DE voice in base models. |
| 2 | Fish Speech 1.5 | Medium–large; GPU strongly recommended (≈10–12 GB VRAM for smooth use). | Low – CPU works but far from real‑time. | No clear German support; mainly EN/zh focus. |
| 3 | Maya1 | Large multi‑billion‑param model; needs high‑end GPU (≥16 GB VRAM). | Very low – practical real‑time on CPU not expected. | Unclear – no solid public info about German at cutoff. |
| 4 | Chatterbox | Several variants; Multilingual / Turbo ≈few‑hundred‑M params; GPU (≈8 GB) recommended, CPU possible. | Medium – Turbo/distilled variant can approach RT on a strong CPU; full multilingual is slower. | Yes – multilingual checkpoints explicitly include German. |
| 5 | Zonos‑v0.1 | Medium–large; designed for GPU inference (≈8 GB+ VRAM recommended). | Very low – CPU inference is slow, not interactive. | No – appears English‑only in public releases. |
| 6 | VibeVoice 7B | Very large (7B). Requires powerful GPU(s), typically ≥16–24 GB VRAM. | Effectively none – CPU real‑time is not realistic. | Likely multilingual, but exact DE status not confirmed. |
| 7 | OpenVoice v2 | Medium; CPU possible but GPU (≈6–8 GB+ VRAM) recommended for cloning speed / latency. | Low–medium – typical CPUs are slower than real‑time; strong CPU + heavy tuning might get close. | Unclear – paper stresses EN/zh/ja; DE status uncertain. |
| 8 | Step TTS Mini | Small / edge‑oriented; runs well on CPU or very small GPU (≈2–4 GB VRAM). | High – explicitly designed to run fast on CPU. | No official German – docs only confirm zh + EN. |
| 9 | XTTS v2 (Coqui) | Medium; GPU with ≥8 GB VRAM recommended for smooth multilingual / cloning use. | Low–medium – CPU possible but usually >RT latency. | Yes – XTTS v2 is explicitly multilingual incl. German. |
| 10 | StyleTTS 2 | Medium–large; practical use assumes GPU with ≈8–12 GB VRAM. | Very low – CPU inference is slow, not real‑time. | Base models EN‑only; DE only via community fine‑tunes. |

  </details>

Basically "we" need is a **misaki[de]** package which generates the phonemes for the written German language. The German kokoro version from tomcle does not do this *yet*, **but** provided the correct phonemes existing models may just work.
/try

**Implementation Plan for #290**

**What needs to be done:**
Add German language support to Kokoro TTS by registering German (`'d'`) as a new language code, wiring it through the G2P pipeline via espeak-ng (which already supports German), training German voice embeddings, and publishing voice `.pt` files to the HuggingFace model repo.

**Files I will modify:**
- `kokoro/pipeline.py` — Add `'de': 'd'` and `'de-de': 'd'` to `ALIASES` dict (line 11); add `d='de'` to `LANG_CODES` under the espeak-ng section (line 28). German will use the existing `espeak.EspeakG2P` fallback path at line 141, no special G2P branch needed.
- `kokoro/__main__.py` — Add `"d"` (German) to the `languages` list (line 23).
- `kokoro.js/src/voices.js` — Register new German voice entries (e.g., `df_*`, `dm_*`) with metadata (language `"de"`, gender, quality grades).
- HuggingFace repo `hexgrad/Kokoro-82M` — Upload trained German voice `.pt` files under `voices/` directory (e.g., `df_clara.pt`, `dm_hans.pt`).

**Approach:**
1. **Code registration** is straightforward: German maps to espeak-ng language code `'de'`, which the existing `EspeakG2P` path already handles. No custom misaki module is needed — espeak-ng has robust German phonemization.
2. **Voice training** is the core effort: generate high-quality German speech training data (likely using a commercial TTS as seed data per hexgrad's established workflow), then fine-tune/train Kokoro voice embeddings to produce `[510, 256]` style tensors stored as `.pt` files. Target at least one male and one female German voice.
3. **Validation**: verify German phoneme coverage against the model's existing vocabulary (`kokoro/model.py` vocab mapping), ensure text chunking at the 510-phoneme limit works correctly for German text patterns, and test end-to-end synthesis quality.

**Estimated time:** 40-60 hours (primarily voice data preparation and model training; code changes themselves are ~2 hours)
/try
/attempt
/try

Hey folks,

Like many of you, I've been amazed by the Kokoro-82M TTS model. But when I tried to find a guide on how to actually fine-tune it for a new language, I hit a wall. There wasn't really a public training recipe available. So, I decided to see how hard it could be to figure it out myself.

After about a week of throwing GPU hours and LLM tokens at the problem, I somehow managed to vibe-reverse-engineer a working training pipeline using a patched version of StyleTTS2. 

The good news: The end-to-end pipeline actually works! Stage 1 training produces intelligible German speech through the standard Kokoro inference pipeline. I've documented all the PyTorch API migrations (like updating weight_norm), token mappings, and training bugs I had to fix to make StyleTTS2 output Kokoro-compatible weights.

The bad news: I am way out of my depth on Stage 2 (the prosody predictor). Stage 2 currently degrades the style_encoder and outputs static noise, likely because joint_epoch=999 leaves it unoptimized while its buffers drift. I built a workaround script that stitches the Stage 1 style encoder together with the Stage 2 predictor, but I don't have the ML expertise to properly fix the adversarial GAN/SLM training loop natively.

I took the time to clean everything up and open-sourced the full training guide, the patched StyleTTS2 submodule, and all my scripts here:

👉 https://github.com/semidark/kokoro-deutsch

If anyone with actual ML experience wants to take a look, laugh at my messy approach, or help figure out the Stage 2 settings, I'd hugely appreciate it. I hope this serves as a good jumping-off point for anyone else trying to train custom Kokoro voices!

/attempt 

Success! We’ve found the training recipe for Kokoro and are now activly working on German voice packs. The scripts and process are in the [semidark/kokoro-deutsch repo](https://github.com/semidark/kokoro-deutsch), allowing the community to create German voice packs or train Kokoro on other data.

Unfortunately, we can’t submit a PR and directly claim the price, since we went beyond the initial goal of funding a German dataset for Hexgard and, by accident, fully liberated Kokoro’s training process. 

Ups... 🫣 I'll take the money anyway 😈

**For context on the timeline here**

On April 10, I published [semidark/kokoro-deutsch](https://github.com/semidark/kokoro-deutsch) -- a complete training recipe for fine-tuning Kokoro for German, including a patched StyleTTS2 pipeline, dataset preparation scripts, and checkpoint conversion tools. I announced it [in this thread](https://github.com/hexgrad/kokoro/issues/290#issuecomment-4223937723) the same day.

Over the following days (April 10-14), I fixed critical Stage 2 training bugs (DataParallel ordering, weight loading, adversarial training), and a community formed around the repo. @dida-80b and @ichDaheim contributed significant GPU time to produce actual trained German models -- here's an [intermediate inference example](https://huggingface.co/datasets/junkstage/kokoro_training/blob/main/bernd_stage1_epoch58.wav). A multi-speaker base model has since been [published on HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/dida-80b/kokoro-deutsch-hui-base).

PR #316 was opened on April 17 -- one week after my repo went public. It adds pipeline wiring and a text normalizer, but no trained model or training recipe. The pipeline wiring (lang_code='d', ALIASES, LANG_CODES) is the same approach I implemented in my fork and which was already described in earlier comments on this thread.

I had planned to submit a PR myself after cleaning up the code from a weekend of intensive work. I'll be putting one together that includes the pipeline integration along with reference to the actual training infrastructure and trained voices that make German TTS functional, not just wired up.
